As of 400 PM Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... A stalled frontal boundary will produce showers and 
thunderstorms over central North Carolina today. Locally heavy 
rainfall and flash flooding will be possible.

A Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5) for both severe thunderstorms and 
excessive rainfall/flash flooding is in effect across central NC 
today. An upper-level shortwave trough and associated MCVs will 
pivot across the region through tonight. At the surface, lingering 
frontal boundary just south of the NC/VA border will interact with 
good diurnal heating and the humid airmass with PWATs of ~2.0 inches 
will continue to trigger multi-cell cluster storms across the region 
this afternoon and evening. The primary hazards will be damaging 
winds associated with downburst and localized flash flooding from 
slow-moving or training storms. Areas across the Piedmont and 
northern Coastal Plain will have the best chance for stronger slow 
moving storms through at least midnight tonight. After the storms 
dissipate and the front lifts to the north into VA, expect low 
stratus clouds to move across the area before clearing skies early 
Tuesday morning. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...  Showers and storms with locally damaging winds and 
heavy rainfall are again possible on Tuesday, but this threat should 
be mostly confined to our north.

Broad troughing over the Eastern US will deepen on Tuesday due to a 
shortwave moving across southern Ontario and Quebec. Weak mid-level 
height falls will result over the Mid-Atlantic, which may reach as 
far south as northern NC during the day. Meanwhile a perturbation 
within the trough and associated weak surface low/trough will result 
in an area of enhanced showers and storms over the OH Valley on 
Tuesday morning that progresses east into the Mid-Atlantic through 
the afternoon and evening. 

The above features will combine with a moist and moderately unstable 
air mass (PW values 100-125% of normal and MLCAPE values of 1500-
2500 J/kg) to result in a chance for isolated to scattered showers 
and storms over central NC on Tuesday afternoon and evening. 
However, precipitation chances will mostly be confined to our 
northern counties as guidance depicts a wedge of relatively drier 
air (PW values of 1.5-2") moving across our south as Tropical 
Depression Two slowly drifts west near the northern Gulf Coast. Mid-
level flow will increase with the deepening trough, and 30-40 kts of 
bulk shear is possible across our far north. Thus the northern 
Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain are where SPC has a slight 
(level 2 of 5) risk for severe weather and WPC has a marginal to 
slight (levels 1-2 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall. However, 
capped POPs at chance given the best forcing will be across VA and 
coverage in the CAMS does not look widespread. Similar to recent 
days, the main severe threat will be damaging straight-line winds.

Additional isolated scattered convection will be possible on Tuesday 
night as a prefrontal surface trough sets up ahead of a strong cold 
front over the OH Valley. Once again this chance is mostly across 
our north, and the severe threat will be less with the loss of 
daytime heating.


KEY MESSAGE 3... Unsettled weather will continue on Wednesday and 
possibly into late week as a cold front approaches and then slowly 
crosses NC.

As mid/upper troughing with embedded shortwave impulses remains in 
place across the Eastern US on Wednesday, a strong cold front will 
approach and then slowly begin to cross central NC from the NW on 
Wednesday evening/night. Weak to moderate instability is again 
expected to develop, though it may be somewhat mitigated by morning 
cloud cover. Still, moisture along and ahead of the front looks 
plentiful with PW values of 2-2.5 inches. So the prefrontal trough 
may provide a focus for afternoon convection, followed by a line of 
showers and storms associated with the cold front moving through 
from NW to SE on Wednesday evening/night. POPs are categorical 
across the entire region, and WPC has all of central NC in a slight 
(level 2 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall. QPF is in the 1-2 inch 
range on average, and locally higher amounts will be possible. Deep-
layer shear of 30-40 kts could result in some storms becoming strong 
to severe, and our entire region is also in a slight (level 2 of 5) 
risk for severe weather. Damaging winds will again be the main 
threat.

Uncertainty increases for late week as models differ on whether the 
cold front is able to push south enough to clear all of central NC 
or whether it will get hung up over our region. Behind the front, 
much drier air will bring clearing and much lower precipitation 
chances. Overall it looks likely for showers and storms to continue 
in our SE on Thursday, but the NW may be largely dry. By Friday and
